title: Microorganisms and disease
blurb: Tell bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and prions apart, match them to diseases and treatments, and explain how infections spread and are stopped.
question: At a walk-in clinic, one patient has strep throat, another has influenza and a third has athlete's foot. Why does only one of them leave with an antibiotic, and what could the clinic staff do to stop these infections spreading?

teach.body: Formal definition: a pathogen is an organism (or agent) that causes disease; virulence is how strongly it does so. The germ theory (Louis Pasteur, Robert Koch) states that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases. Plain English: most microbes are harmless or helpful, like the normal microbiota in your gut that make vitamin K and crowd out invaders. A few cause disease, and an opportunistic pathogen causes it only when the body's defenses are weakened.

teach.caption: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with no metabolism or ribosomes. Retroviruses such as HIV use reverse transcriptase (RNA to DNA). Some viruses go latent: chickenpox virus can return as shingles.

head: Disease
Pathogen
Type
teach.caption: Most UTIs are caused by E. coli. Giardiasis (Giardia, contaminated water) and toxoplasmosis (cat feces, undercooked meat) are also protozoan.

steps.label: 3. Introduced
steps.sub: Causes disease in a healthy host

teach.caption: Other pioneers: Pasteur (pasteurization, rabies and anthrax vaccines), Lister (antiseptic surgery), Semmelweis (handwashing), Fleming (penicillin from the mold Penicillium, 1928), Jenner (smallpox vaccine).

teach.body: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria; they have no effect on viruses. A Gram stain sorts bacteria by wall: Gram-positive (thick peptidoglycan) stains purple; Gram-negative (thin peptidoglycan plus an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide, an endotoxin) stains pink and is generally harder to treat. Overuse of antibiotics and unfinished courses select for resistant bacteria (natural selection), and resistance genes spread on plasmids: MRSA, VRE, multidrug-resistant TB.

teach.caption: Hand hygiene is the single most effective way to prevent the spread of infection in health care. Vaccination protects the susceptible host.

teach.body: Tyler, a nursing applicant, shadows at a walk-in clinic. The strep throat patient has a bacterial infection, so an antibiotic helps. The influenza patient has a virus: antibiotics would do nothing, but antivirals and next year's vaccine can. The athlete's foot patient has a fungus and needs an antifungal. Between patients, staff disinfect the shared stethoscope (a fomite), and everyone performs hand hygiene, which breaks the mode-of-transmission link.

teach.text: Top traps: antibiotics do NOT treat viral colds or flu; viruses are not cells and carry DNA OR RNA, never both; ringworm is a FUNGUS; malaria is a PROTOZOAN (the mosquito is only the vector); Lyme disease is spread by TICKS; TB is bacterial and AIRBORNE; Gram-positive stains PURPLE; antiseptics go on SKIN, disinfectants on OBJECTS; penicillin comes from a FUNGUS.

items: Bacteria: prokaryotic, peptidoglycan, binary fission; treat with antibiotics.
Viruses: not cells, DNA or RNA in a capsid, replicate only in host cells; vaccines and antivirals.
Fungi (chitin; athlete's foot, ringworm, thrush) and protozoa (malaria, Giardia) are eukaryotes. Prions are misfolded proteins.
Koch's postulates: found, isolated, introduced, re-isolated.
Chain of infection: agent, reservoir, exit, transmission, entry, host. Hand hygiene breaks it best.

summary: You can now classify pathogens as bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, helminths or prions, match common diseases to their causes and treatments, and explain Gram staining and antibiotic resistance. You can also trace the chain of infection, name its modes of transmission and choose the right control method.

A.q: Why is an antibiotic not an appropriate treatment for the common cold?
options: Colds are fungal; they need antifungal drugs
Colds are protozoan; they need vector control
Colds are viral; antibiotics target bacteria
Colds are caused by prions with no nucleic acid
A.why: The common cold is caused by viruses (such as rhinovirus), and antibiotics act only on bacteria.

whyNot.0: Colds are viral, not fungal; antifungals treat infections such as athlete's foot.
whyNot.1: Colds are not protozoan; vector control applies to diseases like malaria.
whyNot.3: Prions cause diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, not colds.

A.q: Which disease is caused by a protozoan that is transmitted by mosquitoes?
A.why: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes.

whyNot.1: Lyme disease is bacterial (Borrelia burgdorferi) and spread by ticks.
whyNot.2: West Nile is spread by mosquitoes but is caused by a virus, not a protozoan.
whyNot.3: Tuberculosis is a bacterial disease spread through the air, not by mosquitoes.

A.q: Which statement about viruses is correct?
options: They contain both DNA and RNA
They reproduce only inside host cells
They are small prokaryotic cells with walls
A.why: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: they can replicate only inside a host cell.

whyNot.0: A virus carries DNA or RNA, not both.
whyNot.2: Viruses are not cells at all, prokaryotic or otherwise.
whyNot.3: Binary fission is how bacteria divide; viruses are assembled inside host cells.

B.q: A bacterium appears purple after a Gram stain. What does this indicate about its cell wall?
B.why: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that holds the purple (violet) stain.

whyNot.0: Gram-negative bacteria stain pink, not purple.
whyNot.1: An outer membrane with LPS marks Gram-negative bacteria, which stain pink.
whyNot.2: Chitin is found in fungal walls; bacterial walls are peptidoglycan.

B.q: Tuberculosis can spread when tiny particles stay suspended in the air and are inhaled by people across a room. Which mode of transmission is this?
B.why: Airborne transmission involves small particles that remain suspended in the air; TB, measles and chickenpox spread this way.

whyNot.1: Droplets are large and fall within about 1-2 m, as with influenza and pertussis.
whyNot.2: Vector-borne spread needs a living carrier such as a mosquito or tick.
whyNot.3: Fomite spread is through contaminated objects, not suspended particles.

B.q: Before an injection, a nurse wipes the patient's skin with an agent that reduces microbes. Which term describes this?
B.why: Antisepsis reduces microbes on living tissue such as skin.

whyNot.0: Disinfection reduces pathogens on objects and surfaces, not skin.
whyNot.1: Sterilization kills all microbes, including endospores, and is used on equipment (for example in an autoclave).
whyNot.3: Sanitization lowers microbe counts on objects to safe levels, such as dishes, not skin.

C.q: Using Koch's postulates, a scientist has found a microbe in every diseased host and grown it in pure culture. What is the next step?
options: Find the microbe in every host that has the disease
Give it to a healthy host and watch for disease
Re-isolate the same microbe from the new host
Grow it again in a second, mixed culture
C.why: Step 3 is to introduce the cultured microbe into a healthy host and show that it causes the same disease.

whyNot.0: Finding it in every diseased host is step 1, already done.
whyNot.2: Re-isolating from the new host is step 4, which comes after the host is infected.
whyNot.3: The postulates require a pure culture; a mixed culture would not prove which microbe causes the disease.

C.q: Vaccinating a patient against influenza breaks which link in the chain of infection?
C.why: A vaccine stimulates immunity, so the person is no longer a susceptible host.

whyNot.0: Hand hygiene, masks and disinfecting fomites target the mode of transmission.
whyNot.1: The reservoir is where the agent lives; vaccinating a healthy person does not remove it.
whyNot.2: Portal of exit is how the agent leaves an infected person, such as by coughing.

C.q: A hospitalized patient with weakened immunity develops oral thrush from Candida that normally lives harmlessly on her body. How is Candida best described here?
options: A protozoan transmitted by a vector
A prion picked up from a fomite
C.why: Candida is a yeast (fungus) that is normally harmless but causes disease when defenses are weakened: an opportunistic pathogen.

whyNot.1: Candida is a fungus (a yeast), not a bacterium.
whyNot.2: Candida is not a protozoan, and it came from her own body, not a vector.
whyNot.3: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause brain disease, not thrush.

reteach.title: Intruders, squatters and hijackers
reteach.question: Imagine different kinds of trouble getting into a house. How do the pathogens compare, and why does one key not fit every lock?

blocks.body: Bacteria are intruders who move in and multiply on their own: an antibiotic is the security guard trained to remove them. Viruses are hijackers with no tools of their own: they take over the house's own machinery (host cells) to copy themselves, so the guard who removes intruders cannot touch them; vaccines and antivirals are the defense. Fungi are mold growing in the walls: they need their own treatment, antifungals. Prions are bent furniture that bends the rest out of shape.

blocks.text: The antibiotic guard only removes bacteria: it does nothing against a viral cold or flu.

explain.body: Bacteria: prokaryotic, peptidoglycan wall. Fungi: eukaryotic, chitin wall (yeasts and molds). Protozoa: single-celled eukaryotes. Helminths: worms. Viruses: not cells. Prions: misfolded proteins with no DNA or RNA.

test.q: Ringworm (tinea) is caused by which type of pathogen?
test.why: Despite its name, ringworm is a fungal skin infection (tinea).

whyNot.0: The name comes from its ring-shaped rash; no worm is involved.
whyNot.2: Ringworm is fungal, so antibiotics do not treat it.
whyNot.3: Ringworm is not viral; it is treated with antifungals.

explain.body: Bacteria are living prokaryotic cells with ribosomes, DNA and a cell wall; they reproduce by binary fission. Viruses are a capsid around DNA or RNA (some with an envelope), with no ribosomes or metabolism; they replicate only inside host cells.

test.q: Which structure do bacteria have that viruses lack?
test.why: Bacteria are cells with their own ribosomes; viruses have no ribosomes and use the host's.

whyNot.0: A protein capsid is a viral structure, not a bacterial one.
whyNot.1: Both bacteria and viruses contain nucleic acid.
whyNot.3: A lipid envelope surrounds some viruses; it is a viral feature taken from the host membrane.

explain.body: Pasteur and Koch showed specific microbes cause specific diseases. Koch's postulates: found, isolated, introduced, re-isolated. Lister: antiseptic surgery. Semmelweis: handwashing. Fleming: penicillin from Penicillium. Jenner: smallpox vaccine.

test.q: Who discovered penicillin, and what is its source?
test.why: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, produced by the mold (fungus) Penicillium.

whyNot.0: Pasteur developed pasteurization and vaccines; Fleming discovered penicillin.
whyNot.1: Penicillin comes from a fungus, not a bacterium.
whyNot.2: Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery; he did not discover penicillin.

explain.body: Sterilization kills all microbes, including endospores (autoclave: steam under pressure). Disinfection reduces pathogens on objects and surfaces. Antisepsis reduces microbes on living tissue such as skin. Sanitization lowers counts to safe levels.

test.q: Which method kills all microbes on surgical instruments, including bacterial endospores?
test.why: Sterilization, such as steam under pressure in an autoclave, kills all microbes including endospores.

whyNot.0: Disinfection reduces pathogens on objects but does not reliably kill endospores.
whyNot.2: Antisepsis is for living tissue, and it reduces rather than eliminates microbes.
whyNot.3: Sanitization only lowers microbial counts to safe levels.
